summary.text: Reducing the coefficient expansion modulo \(2\), Lucas’s binomial-parity criterion gives binary containment/disjointness conditions under which the exponent-preserving map \((n,k,j)\mapsto(k+j,k,n-k)\) is an involution on the odd summands. All nonfixed summands cancel in pairs, while an odd fixed point forces \(k=n\) and \(j=0\), and hence \(m=n(n+1)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{r\ge 0}x^r\frac{(1+x^r)^r}{(1+x^{r+1})^{r+1}}
   =\sum_{m\ge0}a(m)x^m.
\]
We prove that if \(a(m)\) is odd, then \(m=q(q+1)\) for some \(q\ge0\).

First we obtain a finite expression for the coefficient \(a(m)\). For a fixed \(r\), the binomial theorem and the negative-binomial expansion give
\[
(1+x^r)^r=\sum_{k=0}^r\binom rk x^{rk}
\]
and
\[
(1+x^{r+1})^{-(r+1)}
 =\sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j\binom{r+j}{j}x^{(r+1)j}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x^r\frac{(1+x^r)^r}{(1+x^{r+1})^{r+1}}
 =\sum_{k=0}^r\sum_{j\ge0}
 (-1)^j\binom rk\binom{r+j}{j}
 x^{r(k+1)+j(r+1)}.
\]
Thus
\[
a(m)=
\sum_{\substack{0\le r\le m,\ 0\le k\le r,\ j\ge0\\
                  r(k+1)+j(r+1)=m}}
(-1)^j\binom rk\binom{r+j}{j}.
\tag{1}
\]
The restriction \(r\le m\) is automatic because every exponent arising from the summand indexed by \(r\) is at least \(r\). For fixed \(m\), the sum is therefore finite. Equivalently, for fixed \(r,k\), a term occurs only when
\[
r(k+1)\le m,
\qquad r+1\mid m-r(k+1),
\]
in which case
\[
j=\frac{m-r(k+1)}{r+1}.
\]

We now recall the binary parity criterion for binomial coefficients. Write the binary expansions
\[
N=\sum_i N_i2^i,\qquad K=\sum_iK_i2^i,
\qquad N_i,K_i\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Then
\[
\binom NK\equiv\prod_i\binom{N_i}{K_i}\pmod2.
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed, over the field with two elements,
\[
(1+X)^{2^i}=1+X^{2^i},
\]
so
\[
(1+X)^N=\prod_{i:N_i=1}(1+X^{2^i}).
\]
The coefficient of \(X^K\) is therefore \(1\) precisely when every binary digit equal to \(1\) in \(K\) also occurs as a \(1\)-digit of \(N\). This proves (2), as well as the equivalent criterion
\[
\binom NK\text{ is odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\mathbin{\&}N=K,
\tag{3}
\]
where \(\&\) denotes bitwise AND.

Applying (3) to the first binomial factor in (1), we get
\[
\binom rk\text{ odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k\mathbin{\&}r=k.
\tag{4}
\]
In words, all \(1\)-bits of \(k\) are \(1\)-bits of \(r\).

For the second factor, (3) says
\[
\binom{r+j}{j}\text{ odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad j\mathbin{\&}(r+j)=j.
\]
This condition is equivalent to
\[
r\mathbin{\&}j=0.
\tag{5}
\]
To see this directly, if \(r\) and \(j\) have no common \(1\)-bit, their binary addition is carry-free, so every \(1\)-bit of \(j\) remains a \(1\)-bit in \(r+j\). Conversely, if they have a common \(1\)-bit, take the least bit position where both have digit \(1\). There is no carry into that position arising from any lower common \(1\)-bit, while adding the two \(1\)'s at that position produces output digit \(0\) and a carry. Hence that \(1\)-bit of \(j\) is absent from \(r+j\), so \(j\mathbin{\&}(r+j)\ne j\). This proves (5).

Reduce (1) modulo \(2\). The sign \((-1)^j\) is irrelevant modulo \(2\). Moreover, each binomial coefficient is either \(0\) or \(1\) modulo \(2\). Let \(T_m\) be the finite set of triples \((r,k,j)\) of nonnegative integers satisfying
\[
0\le k\le r,\qquad
r(k+1)+j(r+1)=m,
\tag{6}
\]
together with the two binary conditions
\[
k\mathbin{\&}r=k,
\qquad
r\mathbin{\&}j=0.
\tag{7}
\]
By (4) and (5), exactly the triples in \(T_m\) contribute \(1\) modulo \(2\), while all other triples contribute \(0\). Therefore
\[
a(m)\equiv |T_m|\pmod2.
\tag{8}
\]

We construct an involution on \(T_m\). For \((r,k,j)\in T_m\), put
\[
s=k+j,
\qquad
t=r-k,
\]
and define
\[
\Phi(r,k,j)=(s,k,t)=(k+j,\ k,\ r-k).
\tag{9}
\]
We check in detail that this is again an element of \(T_m\).

The first condition in (7), namely \(k\mathbin{\&}r=k\), says that the binary digits of \(k\) form a subset of those of \(r\). Hence subtracting \(k\) from \(r\) requires no borrowing: \(t=r-k\) consists exactly of the \(1\)-bits of \(r\) not belonging to \(k\). In particular,
\[
r=k+t,
\qquad k\mathbin{\&}t=0.
\tag{10}
\]
The other condition in (7), \(r\mathbin{\&}j=0\), says that \(j\) is bitwise disjoint from every part of \(r\), and therefore
\[
k\mathbin{\&}j=0,
\qquad t\mathbin{\&}j=0.
\tag{11}
\]
It follows from \(s=k+j\), with carry-free addition by (11), that all bits of \(k\) occur in \(s\). Thus
\[
k\mathbin{\&}s=k.
\tag{12}
\]
Also, by (10) and (11), \(t\) is disjoint from both \(k\) and \(j\), and hence from \(s=k+j\):
\[
s\mathbin{\&}t=0.
\tag{13}
\]
Conditions (12) and (13) are exactly the two binary oddness conditions required of the new triple \((s,k,t)\).

Its exponent is also unchanged. Using \(s=k+j\) and \(t=r-k\), we calculate
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(k+1)+t(s+1)
 &= (k+j)(k+1)+(r-k)(k+j+1)\\
 &= rk+rj+r+j\\
 &= r(k+1)+j(r+1)\\
 &=m.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
Thus the defining equation (6) is preserved.

We also verify the relevant bounds. Clearly \(k\le s=k+j\). It remains only to note that the new outer index \(s\) cannot exceed \(m\). If \(r=0\), then \(k=0\), and (6) gives \(j=m\), so \(s=m\). If \(r>0\), then \(r\ge1\), and
\[
m=r(k+1)+j(r+1)=rk+r+rj+j\ge k+j=s.
\]
Therefore \(0\le s\le m\), and \((s,k,t)\) is indeed among the finite triples relevant to the coefficient of \(x^m\). We have proved that \(\Phi\) maps \(T_m\) to itself.

The map is an involution. Starting from \((r,k,j)\), its image is \((s,k,t)\), where
\[
s=k+j,\qquad t=r-k.
\]
Applying the same construction again gives
\[
\Phi(s,k,t)=(k+t,\ k,\ s-k).
\]
Because \(k\le r\) and \(k\le s\), ordinary subtraction yields
\[
k+t=k+(r-k)=r,
\qquad s-k=(k+j)-k=j.
\]
Hence
\[
\Phi(\Phi(r,k,j))=(r,k,j).
\tag{15}
\]

We next determine all possible fixed points. Suppose
\[
\Phi(r,k,j)=(r,k,j).
\]
The first coordinate gives
\[
r=k+j.
\tag{16}
\]
Since \(k\mathbin{\&}r=k\) and \(r\mathbin{\&}j=0\), we have \(k\mathbin{\&}j=0\). Thus the sum \(k+j\) in (16) is carry-free, and every \(1\)-bit of \(j\) is a \(1\)-bit of \(r=k+j\). In other words,
\[
r\mathbin{\&}j=j.
\]
But membership in \(T_m\) also gives \(r\mathbin{\&}j=0\). Therefore \(j=0\). Equation (16) then gives \(k=r\). Substituting \(k=r\) and \(j=0\) into (6), we obtain
\[
m=r(r+1).
\tag{17}
\]
Thus every fixed point forces \(m\) to have the required form. Conversely, when \(m=r(r+1)\), the triple \((r,r,0)\) does satisfy the defining equation and binary conditions and is fixed; although this converse is not needed for the one-way claim, it confirms that these are exactly the fixed points.

We can now finish. Suppose, toward the contrapositive, that there is no nonnegative integer \(q\) such that \(m=q(q+1)\). By (17), the involution \(\Phi\) then has no fixed point on \(T_m\). Since \(T_m\) is finite, it splits into disjoint two-element orbits
\[
\{u,\Phi(u)\}.
\]
Therefore \(|T_m|\) is even. Equation (8) now gives
\[
a(m)\equiv0\pmod2,
\]
so \(a(m)\) is even.

Taking the contrapositive, if \(a(m)\) is odd, then the fixed-point-free alternative is impossible. Hence there exists some \(q\ge0\) for which
\[
\boxed{m=q(q+1)}.
\]
This is the desired assertion.
